source_text: Ὅθεν οἱ μὲν τὰς ἀγρίας συκᾶς παραφυτεύουσι ταῖς ἡμέροις· οἱ δὲ τοὺς ὀλύνθους ἐκδήσαντες, τῶν εὐκάρπων καὶ ἡμέρων συκῶν τὴν ἀτονίαν ἰῶνται, ῥέοντα ἤδη καὶ σκεδαννύμενον τὸν καρπὸν τοῖς ὀλύνθοις ἐπέχοντες. Τί σοι τὸ παρὰ τῆς φύσεως αἴνιγμα βούλεται; Ὅτι χρὴ πολλάκις ἡμᾶς καὶ παρὰ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων τῆς πίστεως, εὐτονίαν τινὰ προσλαμβάνειν, εἰς τὴν τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἔργων ἐπίδειξιν. Ἐὰν γὰρ ἴδῃς τὸν ἐν βίῳ ἐθνικῷ, ἢ ἀπό τινος αἱρέσεως ἐνδιαστρόφου τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἀπεσχισμένον, βίου σώφρονος καὶ τῆς λοιπῆς κατὰ τὸ ἦθος εὐταξίας ἐπιμελούμενον, πλεῖον σεαυτοῦ τὸ σπουδαῖον ἐπίτεινον, ἵνα γένῃ παραπλήσιος τῇ καρποφόρῳ συκῇ, ἐκ τῆς τῶν ἀγρίων παρουσίας ἀθροιζούσῃ τὴν δύναμιν, καὶ τὴν μὲν ῥύσιν ἐπεχούσῃ, ἐπιμελέστερον δὲ τὸν καρπὸν ἐκτρεφούσῃ. 5.8 Τοιαῦται μὲν οὖν αἱ περὶ τὸν τρόπον τῆς γενέσεως αὐτῶν διαφοραὶ, ὡς ἐλάχιστα εἰπεῖν ἀπὸ πλείστων. Αὐτῶν δὲ τῶν καρπῶν τίς ἂν ἐπέλθοι τὴν ποικιλίαν, τὰ σχήματα, τὰς χρόας, τῶν χυμῶν τὴν ἰδιότητα, τὸ ἀφ' ἑκάστου χρήσιμον; Πῶς τινὰ μὲν γυμνὰ πέπτεται τῷ ἡλίῳ, τινὰ δὲ ἐν ἐλύτροις κεκαλυμμένα πληροῦται; καὶ ὧν μὲν ἁπαλὸς ὁ καρπὸς, παχὺ τοῦ φύλλου τὸ σκεπαστήριον, ὡς ἐπὶ τῆς συκῆς; ὧν δὲ οἱ καρποὶ στεγανώτεροι, ἐλαφρὰ τῶν φύλλων ἡ προβολὴ, ὡς ἐπὶ τῆς καρύας; Ὅτι ἐκεῖνα μὲν, διὰ τὸ ἀσθενὲς, πλείονος ἐδεῖτο τῆς βοηθείας, τούτοις δ' ἂν προσβλαβὴς ἐγένετο ἡ παχυτέρα περιβολὴ ἐκ τῆς ἀπ' αὐτῶν σκιᾶς. Πῶς κατέσχισται τῆς ἀμπέλου τὸ φῦλλον, ἵνα καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἐκ τοῦ ἀέρος βλάβας ὁ βότρυς ἀντέχῃ, καὶ τὴν ἀκτῖνα τοῦ ἡλίου διὰ τῆς ἀραιότητος δαψιλῶς ὑποδέχηται; Οὐδὲν ἀναίτιον· οὐδὲν ἀπὸ ταὐτομάτου· πάντα ἔχει τινὰ σοφίαν ἀπόρρητον. Τίς ἂν ἐφίκοιτο λόγος; Πῶς ἀνθρώπινος νοῦς πάντα μετ' ἀκριβείας ἐπέλθοι, ὥστε καὶ κατιδεῖν τὰς ἰδιότητας, καὶ τὰς πρὸς ἕκαστον διαφορὰς ἐναργῶς διακρῖναι, καὶ τὰς κεκρυμμένας αἰτίας ἀνενδεῶς παραστῆσαι; Ἓν ὕδωρ διὰ τῆς ῥίζης ἑλκόμενον, ἄλλως μὲν τρέφει τὴν ῥίζαν αὐτὴν, ἄλλως δὲ τὸν φλοιὸν τοῦ στελέχους, καὶ ἄλλως τὸ ξύλον, καὶ τὴν ἐντεριώνην ἑτέρως. Τὸ αὐτὸ καὶ φῦλλον γίνεται, καὶ εἰς ἀκρέμονας καὶ κλάδους κατασχίζεται, καὶ τοῖς καρποῖς παρέχει τὴν αὔξησιν, καὶ δάκρυον τοῦ φυτοῦ καὶ ὀπὸς ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς αἰτίας προέρχεται· οἷς πόση πρὸς ἄλληλά ἐστιν ἡ διαφορὰ, οὐδεὶς ἂν λόγος ἐξίκοιτο. Ἄλλο γὰρ τοῦ σχίνου τὸ δάκρυον, καὶ ἄλλος ὁ ὀπὸς τοῦ βαλσάμου· καὶ νάρθηκές τινες ἐπὶ τῆς Αἰγύπτου καὶ Λιβύης ἕτερον ὀπῶν γένος ἀποδακρύουσι. Λόγος δέ τίς ἐστι, καὶ τὸ ἤλεκτρον ὀπὸν εἶναι φυτῶν εἰς λίθου φύσιν ἀποπηγνύμενον. Μαρτυρεῖ δὲ τῷ λόγῳ τὰ ἐμφαινόμενα κάρφη καὶ τὰ λεπτότατα τῶν ζῴων, ἅπερ, ἁπαλοῦ ὄντος τοῦ ὀποῦ, ἐναποληφθέντα κατέχεται. Καὶ ὅλως τὴν κατὰ τὰς ποιότητας τῶν ὀπῶν διαφορὰν ὁ μὴ τῇ πείρᾳ διδαχθεὶς, οὐδένα λόγον εὑρήσει τὴν ἐνέργειαν παριστῶντα. Πῶς πάλιν ἀπὸ τῆς αὐτῆς νοτίδος ἐν μὲν τῇ ἀμπέλῳ οἶνος συνίσταται, ἐν δὲ τῇ ἐλαίᾳ τὸ ἔλαιον; Καὶ οὐ τοῦτο μόνον θαυμαστὸν, πῶς ὧδε μὲν τὸ ὑγρὸν ἀπεγλυκάνθη, ἐκεῖ δὲ λιπαρὸν γέγονεν, ἀλλ' ὅτι καὶ ἐν τοῖς γλυκέσι καρποῖς ἀμύθητος ἡ παραλλαγὴ τῆς ποιότητος.
thought_title: Wild figs help tame figs; nature's hidden wisdom
orientation: Basil is still expounding the vegetation of the third day, drawing moral and theological lessons from the way plants grow and bear fruit.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore some plant wild fig trees beside the cultivated ones; and others, having tied on the wild figs, heal the weakness of the fruitful and cultivated fig trees, checking with the wild figs the fruit that is already flowing away and being scattered. What does the riddle from nature wish for you? That it is necessary that we often receive also from those outside the faith a certain vigor, for the display of good works. For if you see the one in a pagan life, or one cut off from the Church from some crooked heresy, taking care of a self-controlled life and of the rest of good order according to character, intensify your own zeal more, in order that you may become like the fruit-bearing fig tree, gathering strength from the presence of the wild ones, and checking the flow, and nourishing the fruit more carefully. Such then are the differences concerning the manner of their origin, to say the least from very many. And of the fruits themselves, who could go through the variety, the shapes, the colors, the peculiarity of the juices, the usefulness from each? How are some ripened bare by the sun, but some are filled up covered in husks? And of those whose fruit is soft, thick is the covering of the leaf, as in the case of the fig tree? And of those whose fruits are more tightly enclosed, light is the projection of the leaves, as in the case of the walnut tree? Because those, on account of weakness, needed more help, but for these the thicker covering would have been harmful from the shade from them. How is the leaf of the vine split, in order that the grape cluster may both withstand the harms from the air, and receive the ray of the sun abundantly through the looseness? Nothing is without cause; nothing is from chance; all things have a certain ineffable wisdom. What word could reach it? How could the human mind go through all things with accuracy, so as both to see the peculiarities, and to distinguish clearly the differences with respect to each, and to present the hidden causes sufficiently? One water drawn through the root nourishes the root itself in one way, but the bark of the stem in another way, and the wood in another way, and the pith in another way. The same also becomes leaf, and is split into branches and twigs, and provides growth to the fruits, and the tear of the plant and the sap comes forth from the same cause; how great the difference among these is from one another, no word could reach. For the tear of the mastic tree is one thing, and the sap of the balsam is another; and certain fennel-giants in Egypt and Libya weep out another kind of sap. And there is a certain account, that amber is sap of plants solidified into the nature of stone. And the bits of wood appearing in it and the tiniest of animals bear witness to the account, which, when the sap was soft, were caught in it and are held fast. And in general, the one not taught by experience will find no word presenting the operation of the difference according to the qualities of the saps. How again from the same moisture wine is formed in the vine, but in the olive tree the oil? And not only this is marvelous, how here the liquid was made sweet, but there it became oily, but that also in the sweet fruits the variation of quality is beyond telling.

choices.why: The term refers specifically to the wild fig fruit used in caprification, not to the wild fig tree itself
Basil uses it of the cultivated fig's tendency to drop fruit; 'weakness' keeps the medical metaphor of lack of tone
The adjective modifies 'heresy' and carries moral perversion; 'crooked' preserves the spatial metaphor Basil uses for deviation from the Church
The word means a covering or sheath; 'husks' fits the botanical context of fruits enclosed in protective coverings
The standard botanical term for the inner spongy tissue of a stem, matching Basil's list of plant parts
Basil uses the poetic term for plant exudation; 'tear' preserves the metaphor he is drawing on

pass_b_english: That is why some growers plant wild fig trees beside the cultivated ones, while others tie wild figs onto the fruitful, tame fig trees and so cure their weakness, using the wild figs to stop the fruit when it is already running off and scattering. What does this riddle from nature mean for you? It means that we must often draw a certain vigor even from those outside the faith, for the display of good works. If you see someone living a pagan life, or cut off from the Church by some crooked heresy, yet practicing a self-controlled life and the rest of good order in conduct, then stretch your own zeal further, so that you may become like the fruit-bearing fig tree, which gathers strength from the presence of the wild figs, stops its running, and nourishes its fruit more carefully. Such, then, are the differences in the manner of their generation, to mention only a very few out of very many. And who could go through the variety of the fruits themselves—their shapes, their colors, the peculiar quality of their juices, the usefulness of each one? How is it that some ripen naked in the sun, while others are filled out covered in husks? And why is the covering of the leaf thick for those whose fruit is soft, as with the fig tree, while for those whose fruits are more tightly enclosed, the growth of leaves is light, as with the walnut tree? Because the former, being weak, needed more help, while for the latter a thicker covering would have been harmful because of the shade it cast. How is the leaf of the vine split apart, so that the grape cluster can withstand the harms that come from the air, and yet receive the sun's ray generously through the open spaces? Nothing is without cause; nothing happens by chance; everything contains some inexpressible wisdom. What words could reach it? How could the human mind go through everything with precision, so as to observe the peculiarities, clearly distinguish the differences in each case, and set forth the hidden causes without omission? One and the same water is drawn up through the root, yet it nourishes the root itself in one way, the bark of the stem in another, the wood in another, and the pith in yet another. The same water becomes leaf, and is divided out into shoots and branches, and supplies growth to the fruits, and from the same source comes the tear of the plant and its resinous juice—and no words could reach how great the difference among these is. For the tear of the mastic tree is one thing, and the sap of the balsam is another; and certain giant fennel plants in Egypt and Libya weep out another kind of sap. There is also a story that amber is the sap of plants, hardened into the nature of stone. The bits of wood and the tiniest creatures that appear inside it bear witness to this story, since they were caught and held while the sap was still soft. In general, someone who has not been taught by experience will find no account that can set forth the activity behind the differences in the qualities of these saps. Again, how is it that from the same moisture wine is formed in the vine, and oil in the olive? And this is not the only wonder—how the liquid is sweetened here and becomes oily there—but also that among the sweet fruits there is an indescribable variation of quality.

last_rejected.quote: using the wild figs to stop the fruit when it is already running off and scattering
last_rejected.source_quote: ῥέοντα ἤδη καὶ σκεδαννύμενον τὸν καρπὸν τοῖς ὀλύνθοις ἐπέχοντες
last_rejected.why: English says 'using the wild figs to stop the fruit' but source says they tie wild figs (ὀλύνθους ἐκδήσαντες) and use them (τοῖς ὀλύνθοις ἐπέχοντες) to stop the running fruit; the wild figs are the tool, not what is stopped.
last_rejected.fix: using the wild figs to check the fruit when it is already running off and scattering
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly says 'using the wild figs to stop the fruit'; τοῖς ὀλύνθοις ἐπέχοντες = using wild figs to check the fruit.

last_rejected.why: English 'stops its running' suggests the tree stops moving, but ῥύσιν means 'flowing/running' of sap or liquid; the tree checks its loss of sap/fruit, not its own movement.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Stops its running' correctly renders τὴν ῥύσιν ἐπεχούσῃ; 'running' = sap-flow, not locomotion.

last_rejected.why: στεγανώτεροι means 'more watertight/denser/harder-shelled,' not 'tightly enclosed'; the contrast is between soft figs needing thick leaves and hard-shelled walnuts needing light leaves.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Tightly enclosed' is acceptable for στεγανώτεροι; meaning (hard-shelled vs. soft) is preserved.

last_rejected.quote: the growth of leaves is light
last_rejected.why: προβολή means 'projection, putting forth' of leaves, not 'growth'; the phrase means the leaf-covering/protection is light, not that leaf-growth is light.
last_rejected.fix: the putting forth of leaves is light
last_rejected.ruling: 'Growth' is within normal range for προβολή; no meaning change; mere preference.

last_rejected.quote: tear of the plant and its resinous juice
last_rejected.why: English makes 'tear' and 'resinous juice' two distinct things, but δάκρυον and ὀπὸς are in apposition or hendiadys—both mean sap/tear/gum; 'resinous juice' adds a distinction not in source.
last_rejected.fix: the tear of the plant, its sap
last_rejected.ruling: δάκρυον and ὀπὸς are coordinate; rendering both is fine; 'resinous juice' for ὀπὸς is reasonable.

last_rejected.why: Λόγος here means 'account/report,' not 'story' in the sense of tale/myth; this is a reported opinion/theory, not a narrative. 'Story' weakens the epistemic claim.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Story' is within normal range for λόγος; context makes clear it's a report/theory, not myth.

last_rejected.quote: the activity behind the differences in the qualities of these saps
last_rejected.why: ἐνέργειαν means 'operation/working/effect,' not 'activity behind'; the phrase means no account can set forth the working/effect (of nature), not activity behind the differences.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Activity behind' reasonably renders ἐνέργειαν; no meaning change, just paraphrase.

last_rejected.quote: how the liquid is sweetened here
last_rejected.source_quote: πῶς ὧδε μὲν τὸ ὑγρὸν ἀπεγλυκάνθη
last_rejected.why: ἀπεγλυκάνθη means 'was sweetened' or 'became sweet,' but in context of wine it means the liquid became wine (sweetened by fermentation), not that it was sweetened as an additive process. However, 'sweetened' is within range. More problematic: the contrast is between wine (fermented, sharp) and oil (fatty), so 'sweetened' may mislead.
last_rejected.fix: how the liquid here turns to wine
last_rejected.ruling: 'Sweetened' is within range of ἀπεγλυκάνθη; no misleading change; acceptable rendering.

last_rejected.quote: And this is not the only wonder
last_rejected.source_quote: Καὶ οὐ τοῦτο μόνον θαυμαστὸν, πῶς ὧδε μὲν τὸ ὑγρὸν ἀπεγλυκάνθη, ἐκεῖ δὲ λιπαρὸν γέγονεν, ἀλλ' ὅτι καὶ ἐν τοῖς γλυκέσι καρποῖς ἀμύθητος ἡ παραλλαγὴ τῆς ποιότητος
last_rejected.why: English omits the explicit contrast 'here... there' (ὧδε μὲν... ἐκεῖ δέ) that structures the wonder, making the logic less clear.
last_rejected.fix: And this is not the only wonder—how here the liquid turns to wine, and there it becomes oily
last_rejected.ruling: 'Here... there' contrast is preserved: 'sweetened here and becomes oily there'; no omission.
